To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the risk of low birthweight is higher for women than for men; (2) there is a strong genetic influence on low birthweight; (3) there is no evidence for shared environmental influence on low birth-weight; and (4) the genetic risk factors for low birthweight are different for men and women.

(1) low birth weight and type 2 diabetes are both associated with increased risk of cardiovascular disease; and (2) the association between type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease is stronger in those with low birth weight than those with normal birth weight.
the risk of developing T2D was 1.6-fold greater in women with low birthweight compared to those with normal birthweight and 1.3-fold greater in men with low birthweight.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of the environment on the expression of the human genome, and the role of genetic variation in susceptibility to disease.
the effects of low birthweight (LBW) on later life risk of Type 2 diabetes.
the effects of low birth weight on later health and well-being.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there are no convincing epidemiologic studies that support the hypothesis that low birth weight is a risk factor for type 2 diabetes.
there is no evidence that low birthweight is causally related to the risk of Type 2 diabetes.
there is a strong evidence of an inverse association between birthweight and type 2 diabetes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the low birthweight is associated with the development of type 2 diabetes.
low birthweight increases the risk of type 2 diabetes, especially in women.
low birth weight is associated with a higher risk of Type 2 diabetes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the relationship between birthweight and diabetes is not a simple one.
the association between maternal obesity and birth weight is not a one-way street.
low birthweight is a risk factor for the development of Type 2 diabetes in adulthood.
